evidence: Example: a problem-solving method that is purely decomposition. Task T, a problem, splits into subtasks T1 and T2. One edge case: if dividing a task were itself counted as a relation that involves no exchange of information, it would fall outside a. But decomposition passes intent from one level to the next by definition, and that is an exchange of information, so this reading does not create a conflict.

evidence: Example: a lead decomposes a product task and delegates the 'build login module' subtask to Team B. This forms a new working group: the lead plus Team B. G1 adjusts its local parts: a weekly checkpoint as its moment; a commitment to deliver module M, recognised by passing acceptance tests; and an exception rule that a missed checkpoint is reported to G's lead. The agreed defect threshold is 200 ms latency. One defect in M measures 120 ms, so it is tolerable and G1 fixes it at its own level. Another measures 500 ms, so it is intolerable and G1 escalates it to G. This satisfies every clause of (a): a new group per level, base inherited, local parts adjusted. It also satisfies every clause of (b): tolerable defects are resolved locally, intolerable ones are escalated, and the threshold marks the limit of G1's autonomy.

It adjusts the local parts: its own checkpoints (moments), its own deliverables (commitments) and its own exception rules. This satisfies (a). During T1, defect d1 is measured below the threshold, so it is tolerable and G1 resolves it at its own level. A project task is split into two subtasks, each handed to its own subgroup. That makes one new working group per level. Each subgroup keeps the parent's shared vocabulary and reporting channels, and sets its own milestones, delivery promises and exception rules, such as a defect threshold. Statement a holds. In one subgroup, a defect measured below the agreed threshold is tolerable, and the subgroup fixes it itself. A defect above the threshold is not tolerable, so it is referred to the parent level. The subgroup's autonomy therefore ends exactly where tolerability ends, and statement b holds. Nothing in a forbids escalation, and nothing in b forbids inheriting or adjusting the agreement, so every clause of both is satisfied.

evidence: Example: a parent task's working group shares English as its language and a shared chat thread as its channel. It decomposes and delegates the comparison loop, creating a new working group made up of the agent running the loop and the user. That group's own agreement inherits the base: the same language and channel. It adjusts the local parts. Moments: no checkpoints during the loop, so it runs autonomously inside, and one checkpoint at the end. Commitment: deliver the comparison result, with delivery recognised when the user validates it. Exception: if the loop cannot finish, report on the same channel. This satisfies a, because delegation creates a new group with an inherited base and adjusted local parts. It also satisfies b, because the loop is a delegated task with its own agreement, autonomous inside and validated by the user at the end. 'Its own agreement' fits a's inherit-or-renegotiate rule, since that agreement can still include the inherited base.

evidence: The two statements cover different matters: (a) says what autonomy is and what bounds it, and (b) lists the allowed responses to a diagnosis. A single scenario satisfies both. A working group's agreement sets weekly status reports, with one exception: if a report cannot be filed, the issue is referred to the lead. For each task, such as fixing bug X, autonomy (resolving it without referring decisions upward) is one of the task's goals. It is not treated as a standard or a whole, and its limit is exactly that exception. The fix is verified and the diagnosis reads: local scope, low severity, low urgency, tolerable, located in module Y. The response options are only accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent; the team chooses accept. Escalate does not clash with autonomy being a goal, because escalation can be the referral the agreement's exception calls for. Reviewing the agreement fits the definition of review, since the agreement can be the artefact examined after a failed verification.

When a diagnosis arrives, the team chooses from exactly five responses: accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. For a minor, tolerable issue it accepts. For the high-severity case it escalates, as the exception directs. After a failed verification it may review the agreement, treating it as an artefact. Escalating limits autonomy only at the boundary the exceptions set, which is what (a) says, and choosing among the listed responses is what (b) says. Nothing in either statement forbids the other.

evidence: Statement a sorts capability into two kinds: intrinsic or extrinsic to the executor. Statement b only spells out what the intrinsic kind contains. Concrete example: a carpenter (executor) building a cabinet. Their intrinsic capability is their strength and effort (power), how many joints they can work on in parallel (speed), and their choice of which step to keep in mind at each moment (context management). Their extrinsic capability is a borrowed power saw. Every item of capability is either intrinsic or extrinsic, which satisfies a. The intrinsic items are exactly power, speed and context management, which satisfies b. Neither statement limits the extrinsic kind, so both hold together.

evidence: The two statements cover different things. a sets the textual layout of an element: a header with its identifier and metadata, then text. b says how contradiction and redundancy are assessed once elements are written as logical formulas. An element's text can itself be a formula, so both can hold at once. Example: the header line '[R1] {kind: requirement; owner: ops}' is followed by the text 'Order ⊑ =1 hasCustomer.Customer', which is a description-logic axiom. That text runs until the next header line '[R2] {kind: requirement; owner: ops}'. R2's text is 'Order ⊑ ≤1 hasCustomer.Customer', which runs to the heading '## Constraints'. The chosen logic is a decidable description logic such as ALCQ. In it, the set {R2} is redundant because R1 entails it. A minimal unsatisfiable subset would be counted as one contradiction. These judgements are made when R1 and R2 are formalised and are then recorded. They are made again only if R1, R2 or a definition they use (Order, hasCustomer, Customer) changes. Every clause of a and b is satisfied.
